nogpu.about.heading.source: Artificial life, evolving on your GPU

nogpu.about.p1.source: Tidemote is a sealed biosphere of hundreds of thousands to millions of particles, simulated live in the browser with WebGPU. Cells photosynthesize in the tide's moving light, graze, hunt and scavenge, and build their children out of silt. Children mutate into new species, bonded species grow into multicellular bodies, and the climate turns every 10–18 minutes. Leave it running and it keeps changing.

prev.text: Tidemote is a sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the photosynthesizers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view. Leave the simulation running and it keeps changing for hours.

settings.about.p1.source: A sealed biosphere of up to millions of particles, and all of them live, eat, breed, and die in your browser, simulated on the GPU with WebGPU. Some cells drink the moving light of the tide. Others graze on the photosynthesizers, and others hunt the grazers. Scavengers break down the dead and return them to the water as silt, and from that silt the next generation builds its children. Children mutate into new species. Species that bond grow into bodies: filaments, branched fronds, spirals, packed tissues. Some of these bodies grow beating tails and swim. Every 10 to 18 minutes the climate turns, and the world has to begin again in its own way. It makes its own music, too: each cell sings its species' song, over a chorus of the births, kills, and deaths in view.

settings.about.p2.source: No hand steers any of this: every ecological rule is local. The complex interacting colonies emerge from simple rules acting on the mutating genome each cell carries. The Field Lab's <guide>Guide</guide> explains how it works.

matter.silt.blurb.source: Inert mineral grit carried on the currents. Cells build their offspring out of it, and now and then life sparks from it in the light.

matter.husk.blurb.source: The remains of a dead cell. Scavengers feed on what energy is left; the rest crumbles back into silt.

matter.stone.blurb.source: Bedrock, or the skeleton a calcifying cell left where it settled. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Prey shelters in its crevices, and it slowly wears back into silt.

gloss.silt.source: Inert grit, most of the world’s matter. It drifts on currents, every newborn cell is built out of one grain of it, and now and then life sparks from it in the light.

gloss.husk.source: A dead cell’s remains. Starved, elderly, killed and scalded cells all leave one, and eaters drop dung (smaller olive pellets). Holds leftover energy for scavengers and crumbles back into silt after about half a minute: cold water keeps carcasses for the scavengers, warm water rots them fast, and a rotting pile warms its water a little.

gloss.light.source: What plants feed on. It is dim everywhere (how dim depends on the era) and brighter inside tide bands, most of all at the height of the season. You can see it: cells, silt and stone in the bands are lit warm and bright, those outside them dim and cool, and the floor glows faintly where the light falls.

gloss.era.source: Every 10–18 minutes the climate turns: the baseline light and the water’s temperature change, one tide wave is replaced, and the currents shift. In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands; the next full-water era covers them again. Each era is named for what marks it as it begins.

merged.base: Every 10–18 minutes the climate turns: the baseline light and the water’s temperature change, one tide wave is replaced, and the currents shift. In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands; the next full-water era covers them again. An era that warms the water by 5° or more is named Warm or Rising, one that cools it Bitter or Pale; otherwise the names are random labels.

gloss.water.source: The water’s background temperature, set by the climate: it walks from era to era between 4° and 28°, swings ±2.5° with the season, and now and then a heat wave or cold snap passes. Life warms its own water above this: every cell’s spent energy becomes heat, so crowds, bodies and reefs sit in warm patches.

gloss.tidemap.source: The light the Tide brings, right now: dark where it is dim, through violet to pale blue where the bands are brightest. Thin lines trace the bands’ shape at every season, so they still show at low tide, and a dashed line shows where the bands will be in 20 seconds, so you can see where the producers’ light is heading. Tap the Tide gauge (on phones, the era name) to open it.

gloss.maps.source: One map over the view at a time. Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would get there; Heat is a thermal camera, deep blue to teal to amber to white over a span from 2° below the background water to 10° above it, with a line every 2°; Tide shows the light the Tide brings and where its bands are heading. Its key (G, E, H) or gauge opens it, and again closes it.

gloss.thermal.source: How well a cell works at its temperature: a rate that scales its photosynthesis, digestion and swimming. It is at its best within a narrow tolerance of the species’ optimum. Away from its optimum a cell also pays extra upkeep for the stress.

gloss.heatmaker.source: A species that burns extra energy (up to 0.03 per second) as heat. Its cells run warmer than the water, more so in a body, and its colonies warm the water around them. They can serve as lifeboats for warmth-lovers in a cold snap, but they may easily overheat in a heat wave.

gloss.phototaxis.source: Some species sense which way the light grows and push themselves toward it, or, shunning it, away into the dim water. It is a motility of its own, paid for in upkeep, so even a drifting producer can follow the bands of light as they travel; grazers and hunters that follow the light find the meadows there.

gloss.framboid.source: A pyrite framboid: a sphere of tiny iron sulfide crystals, a few microns across like the cells. Framboids grow where a pile of husks rots in cool water (the rot releases the sulfide), and a few lie in the mud from the start. As one oxidizes it warms its water, burning faster the warmer that water is, so a crowded, hot cluster burns itself out. Once spent, it crumbles to silt. Framboids are solid and anchored in the currents like stone.

gloss.flesh.source: Eating other living cells. A cell can only eat species whose surface signature looks unlike its own. Caught animal prey is killed outright and leaves a husk; this takes time, so a hunter manages at most one kill every few seconds. Plant cells are cropped a 0.25-energy bite at a time. Bonded bodies are armored and shrug off some attacks, and an animal hiding among dense producers often escapes.

gloss.photosynth.source: Takes energy directly from light. Light is shared: each photosynthesizing neighbor shades a cell, so a crowded meadow divides its patch of light among many and a thinned one regrows fast (a bonded body barely shades itself). It needs minerals (silt nearby), and runs faster for anchored cells with current flowing past them. Photosynthesis makes a cell heavy: less thrust, no swimming, worse at eating.

gloss.cyst.source: A dormant cell. An animal running out of energy with nothing to eat in reach may go dormant: it leaves its body, stops swimming and pulsing, grays and holds still unless jostled, leaking a little energy, and wakes at random, after about 45 seconds on average. Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.

gloss.stone.source: Bedrock, and the skeletons of calcifying cells. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Attacks made from among stone sometimes miss, so prey shelters in reefs, and calcifying cells settle on their own reef while everything else must go around it. Bedrock lasts nearly an hour. A loose grain of reef stone crumbles within minutes, a grain packed into a reef lasts far longer, and a neighborhood that is mostly reef wears fast, so reefs grow as separate patches and persist only while they are being built.

gloss.calcify.source: How much of a skeleton a cell lays down. Calcifying costs upkeep. When a settled calcifying cell dies of hunger or old age it may leave stone instead of a husk, far more often beside stone already there, so reefs grow outward from rock and from the rare place one starts. Drifting cells seldom leave stone. Calcifiers can settle on stone; to everything else it is solid.

gloss.adhesion.source: How strongly cells of one species bond. Above 15%, each cell keeps up to two same-species partners with springs. Empty slots find the nearest neighbors within bond range; children start bonded to their parent if they are the same species. Bonds last until a partner dies, changes kind or stretches too far away. Bonds are the links you see and they hold bodies together. Bonded cells share the cost of living (up to 15% less upkeep), shade each other less and are armored against attack. They still pay crowding beyond their bond partners, disperse poorly and their inner cells struggle to reach silt to divide. Species without adhesion are single-celled.

gloss.growth.source: How a bonded species builds its body, inherited and mutated like every other gene. Some grow as trees: each new cell buds from a tip at the angle the plan sets, branching every few cells (alternate, one-sided, opposite, or forking), a set number of orders deep, curling or zigzagging as they go, the way filamentous algae, branched cyanobacteria, and colonial ciliates grow. The tips are fed by the cells behind them. Others pack into a tiled mat.

gloss.organism.source: A body: all same-species cells connected through bonds. A species only forms bodies if its adhesion is above 15%; otherwise every cell is its own organism, even when the species has several cell types or gathers into swarms. Selecting a cell of a body selects the whole body: if the watched cell dies the watch passes to another of its cells, and if the body splits it follows the larger part.

gloss.adapting.source: Why the page is drawing less than it could, if it is: frames running late, the GPU busy for nearly the whole frame, the device under pressure (hot or busy, where the browser reports it), or the browser’s own pace (it hands out frames more slowly than the screen refreshes while the page has little to do: only the frame rate is lowered then). With Target fps on Auto it lowers the frame rate to 30 first, then eases what Adaptation may (work done less often, effects, the render scale), and below 30 only once nothing else is left. It climbs back after a stretch with room to spare, 60 fps last. Running fast it does not adapt.

gloss.stride.source: How much simulated time each step moves the world forward. Normally a step is 1/60 s, the most exact. At higher simulation speeds when the GPU can’t keep up, it takes bigger strides per step instead, up to 6/60 s. A device that runs the world at 30 fps needs to double the stride to keep the same speed (2/60 s). Bigger steps are a little coarser and interpolate cell actions, but births, deaths and the variety of species stay roughly the same over long runs.

gloss.mind.source: What this cell is doing, read from a replay of its latest decision. A cell has no brain: every frame it adds up the pulls and pushes of everything within reach (its receptors against their surface signatures, appetite for the foods its diet favors, schooling, bonds, stone), moves, then eats, divides or neither. The mode names which pull wins; hover it for the reasoning. The compass draws each pull as an arrow, its length the pull’s strength, with the cell’s heading dashed and its target as a diamond on the rim. The lamps light for conditions that shape what it does. Fleeing is an evolved aversion: no cell knows what a predator is, but lineages whose receptors happened to push them away from their hunters survived.

Flesh-eaters are drawn to animal cells, grazers (and, reluctantly, flesh-eaters) to plant cells, and husk-eaters to husks. It lets living food inside its personal space so it can reach it. A sated cell feels no appetite.

gloss.colonial.source: On average its cells attract each other. In a bonded species this packs the body tight; in a single-celled species the cells gather into swarms without ever joining.

gloss.solitary.source: On average its cells repel each other, so they spread out (or, if bonded, stretch into strands).

gloss.looseknit.source: Its cells barely attract or repel each other.

gloss.morphs.source: A single-celled species whose genome makes more than one cell type. The types never bond into a body: they are separate individuals of one species with different shapes and behaviours, like castes or life stages. Their children can be any type the developmental rule allows.

gloss.singlecelled.source: Its cells never bond: each one is a whole organism, however closely they crowd. A species bonds into multicellular bodies only once its adhesion passes 15%.

gloss.anchored.source: Barely moves and holds against the currents: a reef or a mat.
gloss.anchored.checkedText: Barely moves and holds against the currents.

gloss.crawler.source: Moves under its own power, but too weakly to count as a swimmer, and is not simply carried by the currents. Any species that is not anchored, a swimmer or a drifter is a crawler.

gloss.focus.source: A highlight: everything outside the chosen filter is dimmed in the simulation.

gloss.links.source: Bonds between cells of one multicellular body. Single-celled species never show links.

gloss.chronicler.source: The chronicler reads the census and a ledger of who ate whom, how each species died and where it lives, and now and then writes what happened in the log: a death worth remembering and its cause, an arms race, hunters and hunted cycling, a lineage following the water, the last of a guild, what an era or an event did. It speaks only when something notable has happened, a few times an hour at most. Lab → Log → Chronicler shows its entries alone.

gloss.card.source: A species card: its portrait, sigil, song, lineage and natural history on one image, with the chronicler’s latest line about it. Save it as a PNG, and its song as a short clip. You can give the species a name of your own there.

gloss.film.source: Records the view as a video, with the auto camera’s captions and the soundtrack, until you stop it (R, or Stop on the red strip). On devices that support it, the film is written to disk as it is recorded. It stops itself before it grows too big (up to 8 GB, an hour or more at 1080p).

gloss.targetfps.source: Frames per second aimed for, as a whole number of the screen’s refreshes so frames stay evenly spaced (60 on a 144 Hz screen is every second refresh, 72 fps). 30 halves the GPU’s work and saves battery; Display follows the screen’s refresh rate (120 on many phones and Macs), which costs the most. Simulated time keeps pace with real time at any rate. Auto aims for 60 and, when the device can’t keep up, drops to 30 before easing anything else, and lower (20 or 15) only once nothing else is left (shown beside Auto); it returns to 60 last, once everything else is back. A rate chosen is held even then.

A rate chosen is held, and then the surface is never turned off for speed. Display → Surface sets how strong it is.

In between, the contacts are carried along, a few frames old at most. Auto looks at half each frame, and Adaptation may take it to a quarter while frames run late (what Auto holds now is underlined). A rate chosen is held.

prev.text: To save performance, this setting can reduce the portion of cells which are checked each frame to determine how many other cells are touching. gloss.splitsteps.source: At 60 fps, where a step of the world does not fit in a frame beside the drawing, the page takes steps of two sixtieths of a second and spreads each over two frames: the view keeps 60 fps and moves on every frame. Auto does this only where it is needed (On beside Auto while it does). Off never splits a step: where frames then run late, the frame rate drops to 30 instead.

gloss.adapt.source: On, when frames run late the page first aims for 30 fps instead of 60, then eases what costs this device most for the least you would notice: work done less often (the water’s waves, cells’ contacts, the stone’s light), the heat haze, the suspension and a little resolution, and only then the microscope, cells’ insides, more resolution and, last, the glow. With room it brings them back the other way, 60 fps last. It eases only the settings left on Auto, in Display and under Pacing (what each holds now underlined), and lists here what it holds back; a value you choose stays as chosen. Off, everything is drawn in full (render scale and frame rate still follow their own settings).

gloss.bloom.source: A soft glow around bright cells, and with it the microscope’s warm halation and the lamp’s veiling flare, which spread that glow. Several extra full-screen passes. Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late, though it keeps it as long as it can (what Auto holds now is underlined).

gloss.neighbors.source: In a crowd, the most nearby particles a cell weighs each step. It samples them evenly and counts each for the ones it skips, so crowding and pushes stay right on average; it only picks food and bond partners from those it saw. The cells it touches (bodies parting, a crowd’s drag) are sampled in proportion. Fewer runs faster in dense colonies and makes no difference in open water. Auto weighs 112 and gives up to 88 or 64 only on a device where the step costs much (no difference to the ecology was found down to 64); the count it uses is underlined. Takes effect at once.

gloss.song.source: Every species has its own song, read from its genome. Its surface signature picks the notes, how it lives sets the rhythm, tempo and range (hunters leap in quick clipped figures, drifting photosynths sway through long ones), and its color picks the instrument. A mutant sings a variation: a few notes moved, or the tune turned upside down, reversed or answered. Its cells sing it as they go, in step if the species schools; a bonded colony adds a second voice.

O turns it off and back on. Its warm glow about whatever is bright is Glow’s.

guide.overview.p1.source: Tidemote is a sealed world on the surface of a torus: what leaves one edge enters the opposite one. Every point is one particle, and the total number never changes. Particles only change form: inert <silt>silt</silt>, living cells, dead <husk>husks</husk>, and <stone>stone</stone>: the world's bedrock and the reefs that calcifying cells leave behind.

guide.overview.p2.source: Energy is the only thing that enters and leaves. It arrives as <light>light</light>, brightest in the bands of the <tide>Tide</tide>, and as the heat of oxidizing <framboid>framboids</framboid>. The energy cells spend on <upkeep>upkeep</upkeep> becomes heat that warms their own <water>water</water>, spreads, drifts on the currents and is lost to the deep; husks rot. Everything you see grows out of a handful of local rules applied to every particle 60 times a second.

guide.cycle.feeding.source: Feeding. Photosynthetic cells drink light; others eat plants a bite at a time, husks, or other cells (flesh), according to their diet. Eaten husks turn into silt; a killed cell becomes a husk, and what an eater cannot digest it drops as dung, another husk. Cells stop feeding once they have enough energy to divide.

guide.cycle.division.source: Division. Once its energy passes its division threshold and a grain of silt lies within about 15 µm, a cell turns that grain into its child and hands over a share of its energy. Every child is built out of silt.

guide.cycle.mutation.source: Mutation. Each division has a small chance of founding a new species with a nudged genome.
guide.cycle.mutation.checkedText: Mutation. Each division has a small chance of founding a new species with a slightly different genome.

guide.cycle.death.source: Death. At zero energy (starvation) or at its lifespan a cell becomes a husk carrying leftover energy. Husks decay and crumble into silt. A settled calcifying cell may leave stone instead, mostly beside stone already there; stone wears back into silt over minutes.

prev.text: Death. At zero energy (starvation) or at the end of its lifespan a cell becomes a husk carrying leftover energy. Husks eventually decay and crumble into silt. A settled calcifying cell may leave stone instead, usually beside stone already there; which forms reefs in the water. Stone eventually wears back into silt over a few minutes.

guide.climate.p1.source: The <tide>Tide</tide> is four slow waves summed over the torus; where they add up, bright bands form and drift. Inside a band it is bright; outside, it is dim but never dark, and you can see it: what lies in a band is lit, the floor beneath it glows and the waves' crests catch it, while what lies outside is dim and cool. <light>Light</light> is what plants feed on: it is dim everywhere and brighter in the bands, and plants crowded together share it, so meadows bloom under a passing band and thin out behind it, and their grazers follow.

guide.climate.p2.source: The <season>season</season> is a 5-minute cycle that swings tide strength between 10% and 100%. This is the Tide percentage shown in the gauge and graphs. The bands keep their shape; only their strength changes. At high tide they are bright and the water is a little warmer. At low tide they fade until they are barely brighter than the rest of the world. This drives the regular booms and busts. Every 10–18 minutes an <era>era</era> begins: the baseline light changes, one tide wave is replaced so the bright zones form and move differently, and two current patterns are swapped. The water’s temperature walks from era to era, so each world has its own thermal history. Each era is named for what marks it as it begins: water warming or cooling, light rising or failing, the water falling to bare the floor or rising over it again, the pool’s last storm, drought, frost or duckweed, or the life that holds the pool (a bloom, a dwindling, hunters or grazers gaining, a genus reigning, a burst of new species). A kind of era that returns is counted (The Second Drowning), quiet stretches take stage names of the world’s own, and the event log says what actually changed.

guide.climate.p4.source: Settings → Map → Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would receive there, with a contour every 10%; Settings → Currents draws the flow that carries silt and drifting cells. The Tide gauge at the top follows the season: the dot rides the 5-minute wave, and the Temp thermometer beside it shows the background temperature, with an arrow while it changes; it breathes during a heat wave or cold snap.

guide.heat.p1.source: The water has a temperature, and most of its warmth comes from life. Every unit of energy a cell spends on <upkeep>upkeep</upkeep> becomes heat in its water, so crowds, bodies and reefs sit in warm patches of their own making. Heat also comes from sunlight (a little), from rotting carcass piles, and from <framboid>framboids</framboid>: grains of pyrite that crystallize in those piles and warm their water as they burn out over a few minutes, so a die-off leaves a warm oasis behind it for a while. Heat spreads a few cells, rides the currents (warm water trails downstream of a bloom) and relaxes toward the climate's <water>background</water> within about half a minute. Stone holds heat: reefs and bedrock warm and cool slowly.

guide.heat.p2.source: Each species prefers a temperature (its <optimum>optimum</optimum>) and stands only so much either side (its <tolerance>tolerance</tolerance>). How well it <thermal>works</thermal> falls off slowly in the cold and steeply in the heat, and narrow specialists work best of all at their optimum, so small differences in warmth matter. Swimmers steer toward water that suits them (<thermotaxis>thermotaxis</thermotaxis>). Far too cold, a cell goes <torpor>torpid</torpor>; far too hot, it bleaches and may <scalding>scald</scalding>.

guide.heat.p3.source: <heatmaker>Heat-makers</heatmaker> burn extra energy to warm themselves and their water. In a cold era their colonies are lifeboats where life keeps moving and singing while the world around it goes still; in a <heatwave>heat wave</heatwave> they overheat from the core outward. Warm water also rots husks faster, so cold eras favor scavengers and warm ones recycle matter quickly.

guide.heat.p4.source: Settings → Heat haze makes warm water waver as if seen through rising heat; Map → Heat (E) is a thermal camera with an isotherm every 2°. Framboids show as brassy beaded spheres, faintly glowing while they burn.

guide.pool.p1.source: The world is a shallow pool under a microscope, a few millimeters to a couple of centimeters across. Its floor has relief: some eras the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands and sandbars. Now and then, about once an hour of world time, the pool suffers an <poolevents>event</poolevents>, announced in the log and on screen:

guide.pool.drought.source: Drought. The water falls until much of the floor lies dry and the pool parts into separate pools. The receding edge sweeps cells along and piles them at the waterline; the mud pales and cracks into plates as it dries. Then rain falls, staining the mud dark drop by drop until it is wet all over, refills the pool, and the resting cells hatch.

They show <cystdry>dried or frozen</cystdry>; most rest as <cyst>cysts</cyst> and wait, losing energy very slowly, and the rest starve. The water's edge pulls cells near it back in. After each event the log tallies how much life and how many species it cost. Rain wakes cysts fast, so a drought ends in a burst of hatching.

guide.cells.p1.source: Each species has one genome. A genome describes up to three cell types, α, β and γ. Each type carries two 8-number signatures: a surface (how it appears to others) and a receptor (how it reacts). The pull of cell A on cell B is A’s receptor combined with B’s surface: above zero means attraction, below zero means repulsion. Silt and husks have surfaces too, so a cell type can be drawn toward silt or repelled by husks.

guide.cells.p2.source: Zoom in to see lobose and filose cells, crooked radiates, incised desmids, horned armour, twisted spindles, slippers, chambered whorls, crescents, stalked bells, bead chains and lattice frustules. Species have their own proportions; individuals have uneven membranes and slowly shifting outlines. A nucleus pinches as division approaches, producers carry chloroplasts, eaters carry vacuoles, and swimmers grow cilia or flagella. These visual forms are cosmetic.

guide.cells.p3.source: When a cell divides, a developmental rule picks the child’s type from the parent’s type. Where that rule settles is the <bodyplan>body plan</bodyplan>, for example α 60 · β 40.

guide.cells.p4.source: Species with <adhesion>adhesion</adhesion> form <bond>bonds</bond>: each cell keeps up to two partners of the same species. New bonds fill empty slots with nearby cells, and children start bonded to their parent, so bodies grow by division. A bond lasts until a partner dies, changes kind or stretches too far away. Bonds are what the links show, so a web of links is one <organism>organism</organism>. Species without adhesion are single-celled and never show links, however closely they crowd.

guide.movement.p2.source: There is no pathfinding and no sense beyond about 60 µm, six cell widths, except for which way the light and the warmth grow. Roamers are swimmers that travel until forces bend their path. Self-propelled bodies come from chases between cell types: if β is drawn to α while α pushes β away, β chases α forever and the body drives itself forward. Evolution keeps whichever pulls lead to food.

Self-propelled bodies come from chases between cell types: if β is drawn to α while α pushes β away, β chases α forever and the body drives itself forward. Evolution keeps whichever pulls lead to food.

guide.ecology.crowding.source: Crowding: cells packed among their own kind sicken (a body’s bond partners do not count), so clonal blobs and sprawling bodies break up and species mix.

guide.ecology.grazing.source: Grazers crop the plants, predators thin out the grazers, and scavengers live off the husks and <dung>dung</dung> both leave behind. Plants share the light, so a grazed meadow regrows.

guide.ecology.fleeing.source: Prey <flee>flee</flee> their hunters and hide among dense producers; well-fed hunters rest (<satiety>satiety</satiety>), so they do not eat each other out.

guide.ecology.catching.source: Catching takes skill: cells catch living prey in proportion to how well they are built to eat it, so photosynthesizers and husk eaters rarely kill.

guide.ecology.familiar-prey.source: Hunters and grazers get good at catching what they caught last and often miss unfamiliar prey, so booming species feed their predators and rare ones are spared.

guide.ecology.heat.source: Heat links species that never touch: a heat-maker's colony warms its neighbors, helping the warmth-lovers among them and driving the cold-lovers away, so species sort into thermal territories of their own making.

guide.ecology.climate.source: The climate keeps changing which strategy pays, and its temperature walks, so the lineages that track it and those that hide in refuges trade places.

guide.ecology.p2.source: Mass is conserved, so every birth needs silt freed by some earlier death or meal. Life is limited by matter as well as energy.

guide.evolution.p1.source: Every mutant founds a new <species>species</species>. Mutations nudge every gene: signatures, diet, swimming, adhesion, color and more. Occasionally a whole cell type is reinvented or copied over another. Most mutants vanish within seconds; those that reach the population threshold become <thriving>thriving</thriving> and are named.

guide.evolution.p2.source: Names are a <genus>genus</genus> plus an epithet. A lineage that drifts far enough from its genus founder starts a new genus, which gets its own new name. Colors are inherited with drift, so related species look related.

guide.reading.color.source: Color: the species, tinted per cell type. Related species share hues. Brightness shows stored energy; newborns flash; some lineages pulse. Heat-stressed cells bleach toward pale bone, torpid ones dim to a cold blue and stop pulsing, and heat-makers glow faintly warm.

guide.reading.shape.source: Shape: disc, ring, star, nucleus or diamond, a lineage marker per cell type. Husks are dim brown rings, dung smaller olive pellets, silt is faint slate. A dormant cyst is grayed and still.

guide.tools.lab-lineage.source: Lab → Lineage: the lineages that held the most life, as a plot of their cells over time (each nested inside the lineage it branched from, so a die-off shows as the whole stack falling) over a tree of the same lineages. A lineage follows a population through species after species; every other species counts with its nearest shown ancestor, and each row says how many species its lineage holds. Click a lineage’s row or its band in the plot to explore it, or drag across the plot to zoom into a stretch of time: finer lineages appear as you narrow in, down to single species. The reticle on the row you point at shows its species in the water, as does each name in an explored lineage’s line of descent. The path above the plot runs from all lineages down through the explored lineage’s ancestors, each a click to go up to; a narrowed span shows beside it, with × to widen it again; Esc or Backspace goes back the way you came.

prev.text: Lab → Lineage: the family trees of the most successful species. A lineage is a line of descent, followed through every species it evolves into. The top shows each lineage’s cells over time, with every branch drawn inside the lineage it came from, so a die-off shows as the whole stack falling. The tree below lists the same lineages, each with a species count. Click a row or a band to explore that lineage, or drag across the plot to zoom into a stretch of time. Smaller branches appear as you zoom in, down to single species. Point at a row and click its reticle to see where that species is in the water. A zoomed time range shows beside it, and × resets it. Esc or Backspace goes back one step.
